prompt: What is a patient-day, as the lesson defines it?
hint: The hospital counts at a fixed hour.

choices.text: A day on which at least one patient was admitted to the ward
choices.why: That counts days, not patients; a full ward and a nearly empty one would score the same.

choices.text: The time a doctor spends with one patient in a day
choices.why: Clinical time is a different measure; the patient-day is about beds.

choices.text: One patient in one bed at the midnight count
choices.why: Right: a month's patient-days over its bed-days is the occupancy rate.

choices.text: A patient's whole stay, from admission to discharge
choices.why: A whole stay is several patient-days; dividing patient-days by discharges gives its average length.

prompt: A 30-bed ward recorded 837 patient-days in January, a month of 31 days. What was its bed occupancy, in percent to one decimal?
Jacarandá's occupancy in November was 85.3%. Why does the lesson say the figure is in a comfortable place it has not earned?
hint: Copy the formula down the wards.

choices.text: Because the midnight count misses the patients who arrive in the morning and leave the same evening
choices.why: Same-day patients exist, but the lesson's point is about how the wards differ, not about who the count misses.

choices.text: Because 85% is too low for a private hospital
choices.why: The lesson treats around 85% as a working ceiling, not a floor.

choices.text: Because November is a quiet month
choices.why: Nothing in the data says so, and a quiet month would not explain a full intensive-care unit.

choices.text: It averages full wards with half-empty ones
choices.why: Right: intensive care was at 98.5% and maternity at 62.3%, and nobody is admitted to the average.

prompt: A board member proposes a target of 100% bed occupancy, "so that no bed we pay for sits empty". What is the lesson's objection?
hint: What happens to the next emergency?

choices.text: A full ward leaves the next emergency with no bed
choices.why: Right: occupancy has a ceiling well below 100%, unlike most indicators in the course.

choices.text: None: an empty bed is wasted money
choices.why: That is the board member's belief, and the lesson's point is that spare beds are what absorbs the variation.

choices.text: Occupancy cannot be measured to that precision
choices.why: The midnight count measures it exactly; precision is not the problem.

choices.text: The target should be set on length of stay instead, since that is what the board controls
choices.why: Length of stay needs its own guard, the readmission rate; swapping targets does not answer the objection.

prompt: Ten emergency patients waited 12 to 210 minutes; the mean is 64.5 and the median 41. Why does the lesson prefer the median for the typical wait?

choices.text: Because the median is always smaller than the mean
choices.why: It is smaller here because the long waits are on one side; with long waits missing it need not be.

choices.text: The two long waits pull the mean up, and no patient waited about an hour
choices.why: Right: the median is the wait of the patient in the middle, which is what a typical patient met.

choices.text: Because the median ignores the long waits, which are not the hospital's fault
choices.why: The lesson reports the long end too, because that is where the harm is.

choices.text: Because a regulator requires it
choices.why: The lesson's argument is about what the numbers show, not about a rule.

prompt: October: 1,310 discharges, 41 deaths in hospital, 112 readmitted within 30 days, 30 of them planned. Leaving out planned returns and patients who died, what is the readmission rate, in percent to one decimal?
Which of these change Jacarandá's 30-day readmission rate, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at what goes on top and what goes underneath.

choices.text: Counting planned returns such as the next cycle of chemotherapy
choices.why: Right: they take the rate from 6.3% to 8.5%.

choices.text: Keeping patients who died in hospital in the denominator
choices.why: Right: they cannot be readmitted, so counting them lowers the rate.

choices.text: Reporting the rate in a dashboard instead of a spreadsheet
choices.why: Where the number is drawn does not change it.

choices.text: Computing November's rate in early December
choices.why: Right: the 30 days have not run out, so the rate is still going up.

prompt: Jacarandá has 32 beds free tonight in total. Why is intensive care the first row of Cláudia's screen?
hint: Which ward needs a decision before noon?

choices.text: Because it has the fewest beds
choices.why: Size is not the order; the rows are sorted by how short of beds each ward will be.

choices.text: Because its patients are the most expensive, so the board wants to see them first
choices.why: The screen is the bed manager's, built for her morning decision, not for the board's costs.

choices.text: It will be one bed short, and the 32 free elsewhere cannot take its patients
choices.why: Right: exceptions first; a total of 32 free beds hides the one ward that needs a decision.

choices.text: Because the screen lists wards in alphabetical order
choices.why: It does not: the rows go from the shortest of beds to the one with most room.

prompt: Why does a dashboard showing November's 30-day readmission rate in early December show a misleading number?
hint: When does the last November patient's 30 days end?

choices.text: Because December's admissions are mixed into November's
choices.why: The admissions are assigned correctly; what is missing is time.

choices.text: Because the hospital closes its accounts only in January
choices.why: The accounting close is finance's calendar; the lag here comes from the definition itself.

choices.text: Many November patients have not yet had 30 days in which to come back
choices.why: Right: the rate keeps rising until the last 30-day window closes in January.

choices.text: Because a readmission rate needs a full year of data
choices.why: It needs 30 days after each discharge, not a year.

prompt: Town A had 252 admissions for heart failure and town B had 190. Why can the two counts not be compared directly?
hint: How many people live in each?

choices.text: Because counts below 1,000 are too small to compare
choices.why: 252 and 190 are large enough; the problem is what they are counted out of.

choices.text: Their populations differ, so only rates compare
choices.why: Right: 76,000 people against 52,000; comparing places means comparing rates.

choices.text: Because one town's patients went to a different hospital
choices.why: The lesson says both towns sent their patients to Jacarandá.

choices.text: Because heart failure is not counted the same way in the two towns
choices.why: Both counts come from the same hospital's admissions, coded the same way.

prompt: A town's admission rates are 50 per 100,000 under 65 and 1,000 per 100,000 at 65 and over. Using the lesson's standard population (85,000 under 65, 15,000 over), what is its age-adjusted rate per 100,000?
Town B has the higher rate in each age group, yet town A has the higher crude rate. Why?

choices.text: Town A's hospital records more admissions per patient than town B's
choices.why: Both towns use the same hospital; the difference is in who lives there.

choices.text: The crude rate was computed wrongly
choices.why: It is computed correctly; it answers a different question from the adjusted rate.

choices.text: Far more of A's people are over 65, the age group where heart failure is common
choices.why: Right: it is Simpson's paradox from lesson 12, with age as the mix.

choices.text: Town B is larger, and larger towns always have lower rates
choices.why: Size alone does not set a rate; the age mix does the work here.

prompt: A rate recalculated as if both towns had the population structure of one standard is called an ___-adjusted rate.
hint: What differed between towns A and B?

prompt: Under the LGPD, what category does data about a person's health fall into?

choices.text: Public data, since hospitals report to the health authorities
choices.why: Reporting to an authority does not make the data public.

choices.text: Anonymised data, once it leaves the hospital
choices.why: Leaving the hospital anonymises nothing; anonymising is a process with its own test (lesson 21).

choices.text: Ordinary personal data, like an address
choices.why: The law gives health its own, stricter category.

choices.text: Sensitive personal data
choices.why: Right: art. 5 lists health among sensitive personal data, and the ANPD enforces the law.

prompt: A published table shows a town's admissions by cause: 21 for one cause, 16 for another, a third suppressed as "<5", and a total of 40. How many admissions does the suppressed cell hold?
Débora works with admissions where each patient's name is replaced by a code, the same code every time. Why is this still personal data?

choices.text: The hospital holds the key that turns the code back into a name
choices.why: Right: that is pseudonymised data, and lesson 21 separates it from anonymised data.

choices.text: Because the data is about health, and health data can never stop being personal
choices.why: Properly anonymised health data stops being personal; the code here does not anonymise.

choices.text: Because codes are too short to hide anything
choices.why: The length of the code is not the point; the existence of the key is.

choices.text: Because Débora is not a doctor, so she may not see codes
choices.why: Seeing a code is exactly the arrangement that lets her work without names.

prompt: A regional health dashboard suppresses counts below five in its default view, by region. Users can filter by town and by cause. What does the lesson say must also happen?

choices.text: Nothing more, since the default view already applies the rule to every region on the map
choices.why: Filtering to one town and one cause recreates the small cell on every click.

choices.text: The filters must be removed
choices.why: Filters are useful; the threshold has to follow them, not replace them.

choices.text: The threshold must follow every filter, totals included
choices.why: Right: suppression applies to every view, with complementary suppression where a total would reveal it.

choices.text: Only staff of the health department may log in, so the public never sees the small cells
choices.why: Restricting access helps, but a staff member filtering to a small town still sees an identifiable count.

prompt: Match each hospital indicator to how it is computed.
Put the steps of comparing two towns with an age-adjusted rate in order.
hint: Rates by age come before the standard is applied.
items: Count admissions and people in each town by age group
Compute each town's rate per 100,000 for each age group
Apply both towns' age rates to the same standard population
Divide by the standard's total to get each adjusted rate
Publish the adjusted rates, name the standard and keep the crude rates beside them
trap: Starting from each town's crude rate skips the age groups, and the age groups are where the comparison is made fair.

prompt: By lesson 17's four questions, what is the typical trap in hospital indicators?
hint: It appeared with beds, with waits and with towns.

choices.text: Measuring too often, so that every small change looks like a trend worth acting on
choices.why: Freshness matters at the bed board, but the recurring trap in the lesson is a different one.

choices.text: Trusting the midnight count, which is too inaccurate to plan beds from
choices.why: The midnight count is the standard, and the lesson builds every bed indicator on it.

choices.text: An average across wards, patients or towns that hides where the trouble is
choices.why: Right: 85.3% hid the full ICU, the mean wait hid the long ones, the crude rate hid the ages.

choices.text: Using percentages, which hide the number of patients, instead of counts of them
choices.why: The lesson turns counts into rates on purpose; percentages are not the trap.

prompt: Unlike most indicators in this course, bed occupancy has a ___ well below 100%, because the next emergency needs somewhere to go.
hint: More is not better past a point.
